fixes.explanation: Few isn't the word Job uses. He says no wonder his words have been rash, because his grief would outweigh the sand of the seas. Rash means hasty, like hitting send before your brain catches up. I think he's owning it a little, and I respect that.

Job says, “…that God would be willing to crush me, to unleash His hand and cut me off!” I think this one hurts. It's a heavy thing to hear a man hope for, and I'd rather sit quietly with it than try to be clever. These are words from Job's reply.

Job says no such thing. He asks, “Is there any help within me now that success is driven from me?” I think the answer he's after is no. I bet a man asking that doesn't feel like he has plenty to spare.
Job asks, “Is there any help within me now that success is driven from me?” It's a question, and I think the answer he has in mind is no. That's a long way from plenty. I bet he feels emptied out.

Job does say the wadis overflow, but this card asks about the dry season. Then they cease, “…vanishing from their channels in the heat.” Nothing in his words has them flooding fields. A stream you can't count on is the picture he gives of his brothers.
Right. Job asks, “Have I ever said, ‘Give me something; offer me a bribe from your wealth…’” I think he means he never said it. It's a question, so that's my read of it.
Fortune isn't what Job says is at stake. He says, “Reconsider; do not be unjust. Reconsider, for my righteousness is at stake.” It's his righteousness he's pleading about.

Job doesn't admit that. He asks, “Is there iniquity on my tongue? Can my mouth not discern malice?” I think the first question means no, there isn't. The second, I think, means his mouth can tell malice when it hears it.

Right. Job asks, “Is there iniquity on my tongue? Can my mouth not discern malice?” They're questions, so this is my read: no iniquity on his tongue, and yes, his mouth can discern malice. He finishes his plea standing by his words.
Right. Job says, “So I am allotted months of futility, and nights of misery are appointed to me.” That's about his own months and nights. Rest and peace aren't anywhere in that sentence.
Job never says he gets up and walks anywhere. He says, “…the night drags on, and I toss and turn until dawn.” Tossing and turning is what he tells us he does until dawn.
Job doesn't say that. He says, “Remember that my life is but a breath. My eyes will never again see happiness.” I think this is a sad moment, and I'd rather listen than hurry past it.
Right. Job says, “Remember that my life is but a breath. My eyes will never again see happiness.” I think this is a sad moment, and I'd rather sit with it than hurry past it.
Job doesn't say the place waits. He says, “He never returns to his house; his place remembers him no more.” Waiting isn't in his words, only a place that remembers him no more.

Right. Job says, “Therefore I will not restrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.” He isn't holding his mouth back. He's going to speak and he's going to complain.
Job asks, “Will You never look away from me, or leave me alone to swallow my spittle?” He's asking God directly. I think he sounds worn out by the long nights he just described.
Job doesn't say messenger. He asks, “Why have You made me Your target…” A target is on the receiving end, and I think that's how Job feels.
Witness isn't the word Job uses. He asks, “Why have You made me Your target, so that I am a burden to You?” Target is the word, and I think it shows how heavy he feels.
Job really does ask it. His words are, “Why do You not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity?” I think that's a bold thing to ask, and I admire him for asking it.
